metadata.title: Shannon Shakes Hands with Chernoff: Big Data Viewpoint On Channel Information Measures

nodes.name: Two data rules of the big data viewpoint
nodes.statement: Two data rules are believed. For one thing, the data does not lie. For other thing, we only need to guarantee that our conclusion is correct with very large probability rather than one in the era of big data [\cite{vapnik2006estimation}].
nodes.statement_short: Data does not lie, and conclusions need only hold with high (not unit) probability.

nodes.name: Mutual information
nodes.statement: The mutual information is a measure of the amount of information that one random variable contains about another variable. In fact, it describes the reduction in the uncertainty of one random variable if another one is known [\cite{Elements}].
nodes.origin_citation: Cover & Thomas, Elements of Information Theory
nodes.genus: a measure of the amount of information
differentia: that one random variable contains about another variable

nodes.name: Shannon mutual information
nodes.statement: According to [\cite{Elements}], the Shannon mutual information is defined as: \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} & I_S(X,Y) = D(p(x,y)||p(x)p(y)) \cr & = \sum\limits_{x,y} {p(x,y)log{{p(x,y)} \over {p(x)p(y)}}} \cr \end{aligned} \end{equation} where $X,Y$ are two random variables with marginal probability mass functions $p(x)$ and $p(y)$ and joint probability mass function $p(x,y)$.
nodes.origin_citation: Cover & Thomas, Elements of Information Theory
nodes.statement_short: Shannon mutual information is the KL divergence between the joint p(x,y) and the product p(x)p(y).

nodes.name: Shannon mutual information formula
nodes.statement: \begin{aligned} & I_S(X,Y) = D(p(x,y)||p(x)p(y)) \cr & = \sum\limits_{x,y} {p(x,y)log{{p(x,y)} \over {p(x)p(y)}}} \cr \end{aligned}
nodes.origin_citation: Cover & Thomas, Elements of Information Theory
nodes.label: Shannon Information

nodes.name: Relative entropy (Kullback-Leibler distance)
nodes.statement: The relative entropy is given by [\cite{Elements}]: \begin{equation} D(p||q) = \sum\limits_{x \in \textit{X}} {p(x)log{{p(x)} \over {q(x)}}} \end{equation}
nodes.origin_citation: Cover & Thomas, Elements of Information Theory

nodes.name: Kullback-Leibler distance
nodes.statement: D(p||q) = \sum\limits_{x \in \textit{X}} {p(x)log{{p(x)} \over {q(x)}}}
nodes.origin_citation: Cover & Thomas, Elements of Information Theory
nodes.label: KL distance

nodes.name: Chernoff information
nodes.statement: Chernoff Information is the resulting error exponent when minimizing the overall probability of error [\cite{Elements}]. As defined in [\cite{Elements}], it is given by \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} I_C({{\rm{P}}_1},{P_2}) \buildrel \Delta \over = - \mathop {\min }\limits_{0 \le \alpha \le 1} \log \left( {\sum\limits_x {P_1^\alpha (x)P_2^{1 - \alpha }(x)} } \right) \end{aligned} \end{equation} where $\alpha$ is real parameter with $0\leq \alpha \leq 1$.
nodes.origin_citation: Cover & Thomas, Elements of Information Theory
differentia: when minimizing the overall probability of error
nodes.statement_short: Chernoff information between P1 and P2 is minus the minimum over alpha in [0,1] of the log of sum P1^alpha P2^(1-alpha).

nodes.name: Chernoff information formula
nodes.statement: \begin{aligned} I_C({{\rm{P}}_1},{P_2}) \buildrel \Delta \over = - \mathop {\min }\limits_{0 \le \alpha \le 1} \log \left( {\sum\limits_x {P_1^\alpha (x)P_2^{1 - \alpha }(x)} } \right) \end{aligned}
nodes.origin_citation: Cover & Thomas, Elements of Information Theory
nodes.label: Chernoff Information1

nodes.name: Chernoff mutual information
nodes.statement: With the aid of Chernoff information to describe the relationship between the two variables, a new mutual information is defined as \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} I_C(X,Y) \buildrel \Delta \over = - \mathop {\min }\limits_{0 \le \alpha \le 1} \log \left( {\sum\limits_x {\sum\limits_y {{p^\alpha }(x,y){{(p(x)p(y))}^{1 - \alpha }}} } } \right). \end{aligned} \end{equation} In this paper, we call it Chernoff mutual information relative to Shannon mutual information.
nodes.statement_short: Chernoff mutual information applies the Chernoff information to the joint p(x,y) versus the product p(x)p(y).

nodes.name: Chernoff mutual information formula
nodes.statement: \begin{aligned} I_C(X,Y) \buildrel \Delta \over = - \mathop {\min }\limits_{0 \le \alpha \le 1} \log \left( {\sum\limits_x {\sum\limits_y {{p^\alpha }(x,y){{(p(x)p(y))}^{1 - \alpha }}} } } \right). \end{aligned}
nodes.label: Chernoff Information2

nodes.name: Shannon vs. Chernoff mutual information: different distance measures
nodes.statement: In fact, both Shannon mutual information and Chernoff mutual information are to depict the inner relationship between two random variables. The difference is that they adopt different measures of the distance between two distributions. The relative entropy is adopted in Shannon mutual information and the R{\'{e}}nyi divergence is used in Chernoff mutual information [\cite{van2014renyi}].

nodes.name: Channel capacity
nodes.statement: For example, the maximum mutual information is defined as the channel capacity for a discrete memoryless channel.
nodes.section: 2 Channel Information Measures and ACE Algorithm Description
nodes.origin_citation: Cover & Thomas, Elements of Information Theory

nodes.name: Binary symmetric channel (BSC)
nodes.statement: Consider the BSC, which is shown in Fig.\ref{fig:channelBSC}. It is a binary channel where the probability of the input symbols is $(\lambda,1-\lambda)$. The transmission error in it is $\varepsilon $.
nodes.origin_citation: Cover & Thomas, Elements of Information Theory
differentia: the probability of the input symbols is $(\lambda,1-\lambda)$
The transmission error in it is $\varepsilon $

nodes.name: Shannon mutual information of the BSC
nodes.statement: \begin{aligned} & I_S(X;Y) = H(Y) - H(Y|X) \cr & = \sum\limits_{k = 1}^2 {\sum\limits_{j = 1}^2 {p({x_k},{y_j})log{{p({x_k},{y_j})} \over {p({x_k})p({y_j})}}} } \cr & = (1 - \varepsilon )\log {{1 - \varepsilon } \over {\lambda (1 - \varepsilon ) + (1 - \lambda )\varepsilon }} + \varepsilon \log {\varepsilon \over {\lambda \varepsilon + (1 - \lambda )(1 - \varepsilon )}}. \cr \end{aligned}
nodes.statement_short: Closed form of the BSC's Shannon mutual information in terms of $\lambda$ and $\varepsilon$.
nodes.label: BSC Mutual information

nodes.name: Chernoff mutual information of the BSC
nodes.statement: \begin{aligned} &I_C(X;Y)=- \mathop {\min }\limits_{0 \le \alpha \le 1} \log \left( {\sum\limits_x {P_1^\alpha (x)P_2^{1 - \alpha }(x)} } \right)\\ &=- \mathop {\min }\limits_{0 \le \alpha \le 1} \log ( {(1 - \varepsilon )^\alpha }{\left( {\lambda (1 - \varepsilon ) + (1 - \lambda )\varepsilon } \right)^{1 - \alpha }} \\ &+ {\varepsilon ^\alpha }{\left( {\lambda \varepsilon + (1 - \lambda )(1 - \varepsilon )} \right)^{1 - \alpha }} ) \end{aligned}
nodes.label: BSC Chernoff information

nodes.name: No explicit solution for the BSC Chernoff mutual information
nodes.statement: Unfortunately, there is no explicit solution for Eq.(\ref{BSC Chernoff information}). As a result, it is arduous to analyze the Chernoff mutual information.\\ It is observed that the Shannon mutual information seems to be completely different from the Chernoff mutual information.

nodes.name: Multiple symmetric channel (MSC)
nodes.statement: The MSC is shown in Fig.\ref{fig:channelMBSC}. The number of input symbol is $M$. The probability of the input symbol is $(\lambda_1,\lambda_2,...,\lambda_M)$ with $\lambda_1+\lambda_2+...+\lambda_M=1$ ($\lambda_i>0$).The transmission error of each one is $\frac{\varepsilon}{M-1}$. The BSC is the special case of MSC for $M=2$.
differentia: The number of input symbol is $M$
The probability of the input symbol is $(\lambda_1,\lambda_2,...,\lambda_M)$ with $\lambda_1+\lambda_2+...+\lambda_M=1$ ($\lambda_i>0$)
The transmission error of each one is $\frac{\varepsilon}{M-1}$

nodes.name: Shannon mutual information of the MSC
nodes.statement: \begin{aligned} & I_S(X;Y) = D(p(x,y)||p(x)p(y)) \cr & = \sum\limits_{k = 1}^M {\sum\limits_{j = 1}^M {p({x_k},{y_j})log{{p({x_k},{y_j})} \over {p({x_k})p({y_j})}}} } \cr \end{aligned}
nodes.label: MSC Mutual information

nodes.name: Chernoff mutual information of the MSC
nodes.statement: \begin{aligned} &I_C(X;Y)=- \mathop {\min }\limits_{0 \le \alpha \le 1} \log \left( {\sum\limits_x {{p(xy)}^\alpha (x){(p(x)p(y))}^{1 - \alpha }(x)} } \right)\\ \end{aligned}
nodes.label: MSC Chernoff information

nodes.name: ACE residual error
nodes.statement: Assume random variables $X_1,X_2,\cdots ,X_p$ are predictors and $Y$ is response. Supposing $\phi _1(X_1),\phi _2(X_2),\cdots,\phi _p(X_p),\theta (Y)$ are arbitrary zero mean functions of the corresponding variables, the residual error is \begin{equation} {e^2}\left( {\theta ,{\phi _1},\cdots,{\phi _p}} \right) = {{E\left\{ {{{\left[ {\theta (Y) - \sum\limits_{i = 1}^p {{\phi _i}({X_i})} } \right]}^2}} \right\}} \over {E\left[ {{\theta ^2}(Y)} \right]}} \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Normalised mean squared error between $\theta(Y)$ and the additive fit $\sum_i \phi_i(X_i)$.

nodes.name: ACE Algorithm
nodes.statement: \caption{ACE Algorithm} \begin{algorithmic}[1] \STATE set $\theta (Y) = Y/\left\| Y \right\|$ and ${\phi _1}({X_1}),...,{\phi _p}({X_p}) = 0$;\\ \STATE Iterate until $e^2(\theta,\phi_1,...,\phi_p)$fails to decrease;\\ \STATE Iterate until $e^2(\theta,\phi_1,...,\phi_p)$fails to decrease;\\ \STATE For $k=1$ to p Do:\\ \begin{equation*} {\phi _{k,1}}({X_k}) = E\left[ {\theta (Y) - \sum\limits_{i \ne k} {{\phi _i}\left( {{X_i}} \right)} \left| {{X_k}} \right.} \right]; \end{equation*} replace $\phi_k(X_k)$ with $\phi_{k,1}(X_k)$;\\ End For Loop;\\ \STATE End Inner Iteration Loop;\\ \STATE \begin{equation*} {\theta _1}(Y) = {{E\left[ {\sum\limits_{i = 1} {{\phi _i}({X_i})\left| Y \right.} } \right]} \over {\left\| {E\left[ {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^p {{\phi _i}({X_i})\left| Y \right.} } \right]} \right\|}}; \end{equation*} replace $\theta(Y)$ with $\theta_1(Y)$;\\ \STATE End Outer Iteration Loop;\\ \STATE $\theta,\phi_1,...,\phi_p$ are the solution $\theta^*,\phi^*_1,...,\phi^*_p$;\\ \end{algorithmic}
nodes.statement_short: Alternating conditional expectations: alternately update each $\phi_k$ and $\theta$ by conditional expectations until the residual error stops decreasing.
nodes.label: alg:ACE

nodes.name: Initialise transformations
nodes.statement: set $\theta (Y) = Y/\left\| Y \right\|$ and ${\phi _1}({X_1}),...,{\phi _p}({X_p}) = 0$;\\
nodes.statement_short: Initialise $\theta$ to normalised $Y$ and all $\phi_k$ to zero.

nodes.name: Outer iteration loop
nodes.statement: Iterate until $e^2(\theta,\phi_1,...,\phi_p)$fails to decrease;\\
nodes.statement_short: Outer loop until the residual error stops decreasing.

nodes.name: Inner iteration loop
nodes.statement: Iterate until $e^2(\theta,\phi_1,...,\phi_p)$fails to decrease;\\
nodes.statement_short: Inner loop until the residual error stops decreasing.

nodes.name: Backfitting loop over predictors
nodes.statement: For $k=1$ to p Do:\\ \begin{equation*} {\phi _{k,1}}({X_k}) = E\left[ {\theta (Y) - \sum\limits_{i \ne k} {{\phi _i}\left( {{X_i}} \right)} \left| {{X_k}} \right.} \right]; \end{equation*} replace $\phi_k(X_k)$ with $\phi_{k,1}(X_k)$;\\ End For Loop;\\
nodes.statement_short: For each predictor, replace $\phi_k$ by the conditional expectation of the partial residual given $X_k$.

nodes.name: End inner loop
nodes.statement: End Inner Iteration Loop;\\
nodes.statement_short: Close the inner loop.

nodes.name: Update theta
nodes.statement: \begin{equation*} {\theta _1}(Y) = {{E\left[ {\sum\limits_{i = 1} {{\phi _i}({X_i})\left| Y \right.} } \right]} \over {\left\| {E\left[ {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^p {{\phi _i}({X_i})\left| Y \right.} } \right]} \right\|}}; \end{equation*} replace $\theta(Y)$ with $\theta_1(Y)$;\\
nodes.statement_short: Update $\theta$ to the normalised conditional expectation of $\sum_i\phi_i$ given $Y$.

nodes.name: End outer loop
nodes.statement: End Outer Iteration Loop;\\
nodes.statement_short: Close the outer loop.

nodes.name: Return solution
nodes.statement: $\theta,\phi_1,...,\phi_p$ are the solution $\theta^*,\phi^*_1,...,\phi^*_p$;\\
nodes.statement_short: Return the converged transformations as the optimal ones.

nodes.name: Channel information as a function of channel parameters
nodes.label: Eq ACE Alg4

nodes.name: Channel parameters known and independent; f known
nodes.statement: It is supposed that ${X_1},{X_2},...,{X_p}$ are known and independent. Moreover, the functional relation $f$ is also known since it is defined by human to describe the channel information.

nodes.name: ACE additive decomposition of channel information
nodes.statement: \theta (Y) = \sum\limits_{i = 1}^p {{\phi _i}(X_i)} + \delta
nodes.statement_short: $\theta(Y)$ equals the sum of per-parameter transforms $\phi_i(X_i)$ plus residual $\delta$.
nodes.label: ACE_Def

nodes.name: Simulation Procedure
nodes.statement: \caption*{Simulation Procedure} \begin{algorithmic}[1] \STATE Generate channel parameters, such as $\lambda$ and $\varepsilon$; \STATE Calculate the channel information measures, such as Shannon mutual information; \STATE Decompose these channel information measures by ACE algorithm; \STATE Repeat above process till the required times. \end{algorithmic}
nodes.statement_short: Monte Carlo: sample channel parameters, compute information measures, decompose with ACE, repeat.
output: Decompose these channel information measures by ACE algorithm
nodes.label: alg:simulated

nodes.name: Generate parameters
nodes.statement: Generate channel parameters, such as $\lambda$ and $\varepsilon$;
nodes.statement_short: Sample channel parameters.

nodes.name: Compute measures
nodes.statement: Calculate the channel information measures, such as Shannon mutual information;
nodes.statement_short: Compute information measures.

nodes.name: ACE decomposition
nodes.statement: Decompose these channel information measures by ACE algorithm;
nodes.statement_short: Run ACE on the measures.

nodes.name: Repeat
nodes.statement: Repeat above process till the required times.
nodes.statement_short: Repeat the procedure as many times as needed.

nodes.name: BSC simulation
nodes.statement: $20000$ observations geneated from the Eq.(\ref{BSC Mutual information}) and Eq.(\ref{BSC Chernoff information}) where $\lambda$ is the probability of the input symbol and $\varepsilon$ is the transmission error. $\lambda$ and $\varepsilon$ are independently drawn from a uniform distribution $U(0,1)$. In this case, our channel information is a multivariate case with two input parameters.

nodes.name: BSC: ACE transformations coincide for Shannon and Chernoff
nodes.statement: It is noted that function curve of $\phi_1(\lambda)$ and $\phi_2(\varepsilon)$ w.r.t. Shannon mutual information is almost coincided with that w.r.t Chernoff mutual information after the ACE decomposition. As a result, in the range of the errors permitted, the $\phi_1(\lambda)$ and $\phi_2(\varepsilon)$ appears to be coincided with each other.
assumptions: $\lambda$ and $\varepsilon$ are independently drawn from a uniform distribution $U(0,1)$
conclusions: function curve of $\phi_1(\lambda)$ and $\phi_2(\varepsilon)$ w.r.t. Shannon mutual information is almost coincided with that w.r.t Chernoff mutual information after the ACE decomposition
nodes.statement_short: In the BSC, ACE parameter transforms are nearly identical for Shannon and Chernoff mutual information.

nodes.name: BSC: Shannon smaller than Chernoff with identical trend
nodes.statement: The results of Shannon mutual information are smaller than the Chernoff mutual information, but whole variant trend is identical. $\theta(y)$ increases rapidly when $y$ is close to zero and the slope of its curve is becoming smaller as $y$ increases.
assumptions: $\lambda$ and $\varepsilon$ are independently drawn from a uniform distribution $U(0,1)$
conclusions: The results of Shannon mutual information are smaller than the Chernoff mutual information, but whole variant trend is identical.

nodes.name: MSC simulation
nodes.statement: $60000$ observations generated from the Eq.(\ref{MSC Mutual information}) and Eq.(\ref{MSC Chernoff information}) where $\lambda_1,\lambda_2,\lambda_3$ is the probability of the input symbol and $\varepsilon$ is the transmission error. They are generated randomly and independently, which is bound in $(0,1)$. In this case, our channel information is a multivariate case with four input parameters.

nodes.name: MSC: ACE transformations almost the same for Shannon and Chernoff
nodes.statement: It is obviously that the function curves of $\theta(y)$,$\phi_1(\lambda_1)$,$\phi_2(\lambda_2)$,$\phi_3(\lambda_3)$ and $\phi_4(\varepsilon)$ are almost the same for these two channel information measures.
assumptions: They are generated randomly and independently, which is bound in $(0,1)$.
conclusions: the function curves of $\theta(y)$,$\phi_1(\lambda_1)$,$\phi_2(\lambda_2)$,$\phi_3(\lambda_3)$ and $\phi_4(\varepsilon)$ are almost the same for these two channel information measures

nodes.name: MSC: Shannon smaller than Chernoff with identical trend
nodes.statement: the result of Shannon mutual information is smaller than the Chernoff mutual information, but whole varying trend is identical. $\theta(y)$ increases rapidly when $y$ is also close to zero and the slope of its curve is becoming smaller as $y$ increases.
assumptions: They are generated randomly and independently, which is bound in $(0,1)$.
conclusions: the result of Shannon mutual information is smaller than the Chernoff mutual information, but whole varying trend is identical.

nodes.name: PAC model suffices
nodes.statement: In fact, the probably approximately correct (PAC) model is enough for us in most of time [\cite{vapnik2006estimation}]. In this model, one only need to construct algorithms which guarantee that it is correct with high probability (not necessarily one).

nodes.name: ACE result as compound function
nodes.statement: \begin{aligned} Y = f\left( {\textbf{X}} \right) \overset{(a)}{=}{\theta ^{ - 1}}\left( {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^p {{\phi _i}({X_i})} } \right)= \psi \left( {\varphi \left( { {\textbf{X}} } \right)} \right)\\ \end{aligned}
nodes.statement_short: Channel information equals $\theta^{-1}$ of the additive parameter transform, i.e. $\psi(\varphi(\mathbf{X}))$.
nodes.label: Res_Fun

nodes.name: Parameter transforms identical for Shannon and Chernoff
nodes.statement: From the figures above, it is noted that $ \phi_i(X_i)$ is almost the same for both Shannon and Chernoff mutual information. For these two measures, the only difference is $\theta(\cdot)$. The function $\psi(\cdot)$ is different and ${\varphi \left( { {\textbf{X}} } \right)} $ is the same.
assumptions: $Y$ is the channel information and ${\textbf{X}}$ is all the set of all the input channel parameters
conclusions: $ \phi_i(X_i)$ is almost the same for both Shannon and Chernoff mutual information
The function $\psi(\cdot)$ is different and ${\varphi \left( { {\textbf{X}} } \right)} $ is the same.
nodes.statement_short: Only $\theta$ (hence $\psi$) differs between Shannon and Chernoff; the parameter part $\varphi(\mathbf{X})$ is shared.

nodes.name: Shannon's inverse transform exceeds Chernoff's
nodes.statement: it is also noted that the function $\theta(\cdot)$ is monotonic function. As mentioned above, the curves of $\theta(\cdot)$ have the same trend and the values of $\theta(Y)$ for Shannon mutual information is invariably smaller than those for Chernoff information. Therefore, the Shannon's $\theta^{-1}(\cdot)$ is bigger than Chernoff's.
assumptions: the values of $\theta(Y)$ for Shannon mutual information is invariably smaller than those for Chernoff information
conclusions: the Shannon's $\theta^{-1}(\cdot)$ is bigger than Chernoff's

nodes.name: KL divergence is the special case of Rényi divergence at alpha=1
nodes.statement: Over the last decades, Shannon information and Chernoff information are always considered to be two kinds of channel information measures and the relation between them is that Kullback-Leibler divergence is the special case of R{\'{e}}nyi divergence when $\alpha=1$.

nodes.name: Shannon shakes hands with Chernoff
nodes.statement: However, with the aid of the ACE algorithm, we find the inner relations between them. In fact, they are different metrics of the same physical quantity. For a channel, in a certain time, if all of its parameters are given, all of its state and properties will be determined. Thus the information about the same channel is always consistent.
assumptions: For a channel, in a certain time, if all of its parameters are given, all of its state and properties will be determined.
conclusions: In fact, they are different metrics of the same physical quantity.
nodes.statement_short: Shannon and Chernoff mutual information are different metrics of the same physical quantity.

nodes.name: Kilometer and centimeter analogy
nodes.statement: For example, the kilometer and centimeter are both measures of length, but they are used in different situations for convenience. Generally speaking, we do not adopt the centimeter to measure the distance between two cities. In contrast, we would like adopt it to measure the length of the steel rule. Their true values are identical when measuring the same things, even their numerical values are different. Similarly, the Shannon and Chernoff information are two metrics of the same quantity of information.

nodes.name: Nature of channel information
nodes.statement: It is noted that $\varphi \left( {\textbf{X}}\right)$ in Eq.(\ref{Res_Fun}) is the same whatever we adopt the Shannon channel information measures or Chernoff channel information measures. In this paper, we take $\varphi \left( {\textbf{X}}\right)$ as the nature of channel information and we get \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} \varPsi=\varphi \left( {\textbf{X}} \right) \end{aligned} \end{equation} where the $\varPsi$ is the nature of channel information. It is only decided by the channel parameters and it contains the core of the channel information.
nodes.statement_short: The nature of channel information $\varPsi=\varphi(\mathbf{X})$ is the measure-independent part of the ACE decomposition, determined by channel parameters only.

nodes.name: Nature of channel information
nodes.statement: \begin{aligned} \varPsi=\varphi \left( {\textbf{X}} \right) \end{aligned}
nodes.label: Nature_Fun

nodes.name: Channel information measures are functions of the nature
nodes.statement: The other physical quantity about channel information is just the function of $\varPsi$, just as \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} \rm{I}= \psi (\varPsi) \end{aligned} \end{equation} where $\rm{I}$ is a measurement of channel information.
assumptions: $\rm{I}$ is a measurement of channel information
conclusions: The other physical quantity about channel information is just the function of $\varPsi$

nodes.name: Measure as function of the nature
nodes.statement: \begin{aligned} \rm{I}= \psi (\varPsi) \end{aligned}
nodes.label: Nature_Fun1

nodes.name: Nature of channel information conjecture
nodes.statement: There is a conjecture that if a novel information measure is put forward to measure the channel information, it will be decomposed to a function of $\psi(\cdot)$ by ACE algorithm from a very large extent.
assumptions: a novel information measure is put forward to measure the channel information
conclusions: it will be decomposed to a function of $\psi(\cdot)$ by ACE algorithm from a very large extent
nodes.statement_short: Any new channel information measure decomposes via ACE into some $\psi$ of the same nature $\varPsi$.

nodes.name: Criterion for new information measures
nodes.statement: This rule can be used to judge the rationality of the new information measure. This conjecture also provides a way for us to propose a new information measure for the fact that we can construct that based on designing the function $\psi(\cdot)$.
